```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

A forecast continues from some level in the last observed year, the
*jump-off*. Most models start from their own fitted rates of that year,
which differ from the observed rates: a model with few parameters does not
reproduce every age, year and stratum. The difference shows up as a step
between the last observed and the first forecast year. This vignette
shows when the step is large, the three ways of placing the start, and
what they change.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
```

## When the step is large

The step is the distance between the model's fitted rates and the
observed rates in the last year. Lee-Carter fitted to each stratum
separately has an age pattern and a period index of its own for every
stratum and follows each year closely. Li-Lee pools the quintiles of each
sex: they share one trend and deviate from it by a stationary factor, so
the fit of a single quintile in a single year is looser.
`mt_jump_off()` reports life expectancy at birth in the last observed year
(2019), as fitted, and in the first forecast year:

```{r}
fc_lc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), h = 10, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
fc_ll <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), x), h = 10, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
merge(mt_jump_off(fc_lc)[, .(label, observed, lee_carter_fitted = fitted)],
      mt_jump_off(fc_ll)[, .(label, li_lee_fitted = fitted, li_lee_2020 = forecast)], by = "label")[
  , lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v, 2) else v)]
```

Lee-Carter reproduces the observed life expectancy of 2019 to a few
hundredths of a year. Li-Lee puts women in Q1 0.4 years above the observed
value and women in Q5 0.3 years below it: it pulls the quintiles towards
their common trend. For women in Q1 its first forecast year then adds
another 0.7 years. The step carries into every forecast year.

## Three starting points

* **fitted** (default): the forecast continues from the model's fitted
  rates of the last year;
* **observed**: it continues from the observed rates of the last year
  (`li_lee(jump_off = "observed")`, `lee_carter(jump_off = "observed")`),
  with all their noise;
* **anchored**: `anchored()` moves the start of any model to the observed
  level of the last years (by default three), shrinks the offsets of
  cells with few deaths towards the mean of the stratum, and lets the
  offsets fade out over `decay` years (by default ten), so that the
  forecast returns to the model's trend.

```{r}
fc <- list(fitted = fc_ll,
           observed = mt_forecast(mt_fit(li_lee(common_by = "sex", jump_off = "observed"), x), h = 10,
                                  n_draws = 500, seed = 1),
           anchored = mt_forecast(mt_fit(anchored(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), years = 3), x), h = 10,
                                  n_draws = 500, seed = 1))
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 4}
mt_plot_compare(fc, strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5"), periods = c(2010, 2029), data = x)
```

The solid line is the fitted Li-Lee model, the points the observed life
expectancy. The fitted forecast continues from the solid line, above the
last points for women in Q1. The observed and the anchored forecasts start
at the observed level. By age, the observed start also carries the noise
of single cells, which the anchored start averages over three years:

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 5}
mt_plot_compare(fc, quantity = "rate", ages = c("45-49", "65-69", "85-89"), strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5"),
                periods = c(2010, 2025))
```

## Which start forecasts better

A backtest fits each version to the years up to an origin and scores the
following five years:

```{r}
bt <- mt_compare(list(fitted = li_lee(common_by = "sex"), observed = li_lee(common_by = "sex", jump_off = "observed"),
                      anchored = anchored(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), years = 3)),
                 x, origins = 2008:2014, h = 5, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy")
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "cov95"))
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
mt_plot_scores(bt, target = "life_expectancy")
```

`crps` scores the log death rates, `crps_le` life expectancy at birth in
years (lower is better; see "Backtesting and scores"). The anchored start
gives the most accurate forecasts of the rates and of life expectancy.
The observed start forecasts life expectancy about as well but the rates
worse, because it carries the noise of single ages and years into the
forecast. For Lee-Carter fitted to each stratum, whose step is small here,
the fitted and the anchored start give the same scores (CRPS 0.068) and
the observed start a worse one (0.078).

## Summary

| Start | How | When |
|---|---|---|
| fitted | default of every model | the model fits the last years closely |
| observed | `jump_off = "observed"` of `lee_carter()` and `li_lee()` | large populations with little noise |
| anchored | `anchored(model, years = 3, decay = 10)` around any model | pooled or smooth models; noisy last years |

`mt_jump_off()` shows the step of any forecast; a backtest shows whether
another start forecasts better on the data at hand.
